cards.a: 802.11 is the IEEE standard family for WLANs. It defines the MAC and PHY layers, the management frames that run association, and the amendment generations (a/b/g/n/ac/ax) that add speed and bands.

cards.q: What are the three 802.11 frame types and what do they do?
cards.a: Management frames (beacon, probe, auth, assoc) run the association lifecycle; control frames (RTS/CTS, ACK) manage the medium; data frames carry the payload.

cards.q: How does the CSMA/CA access mechanism work?
cards.a: A station listens to sense the channel, waits a random backoff (DIFS/AIFS), sends when the channel is clear, and the receiver confirms with an ACK.

cards.q: Why does wireless use CSMA/CA with ACKs instead of collision detection?
cards.a: Wireless stations cannot detect collisions while transmitting in the shared RF medium, so they use carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) and have the receiver confirm receipt with an ACK.

cards.q: What is the management frame flow for a station joining a WLAN?
cards.a: Beacon (AP to STA) for discovery, probe request/response for searching, authentication for identity, then association to join the BSS.

cards.q: How often do APs send beacons and what do they advertise?
cards.a: APs send beacons roughly every 100 ms to advertise the BSSID/SSID and the presence of the network for discovery.

cards.q: What are the legacy 802.11 amendments b, a, and g and their speeds?
cards.a: 802.11b uses 2.4 GHz at 11 Mbps; 802.11a uses 5 GHz at 54 Mbps; 802.11g uses 2.4 GHz at 54 Mbps. All are legacy amendments.

cards.q: What are the modern 802.11 amendments n, ac, and ax and their key features?
cards.a: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) uses 2.4/5 GHz at up to 600 Mbps with MIMO; 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) uses 5 GHz at ~1.7 Gbps with wide channels; 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) uses 2.4/5/6 GHz at ~9.6 Gbps with OFDMA.

cards.q: What is the exam mnemonic for the 802.11 amendments?
cards.a: n = MIMO; ac = 5 GHz fast with wide channels; ax = OFDMA and 6 GHz support.

cards.q: What do RTS, CTS, and NAV do in 802.11?
cards.a: RTS (request to send) reserves the medium, CTS (clear to send) grants it, and NAV is the wait timer stations honor. RTS/CTS mitigates hidden-node problems.
It mitigates hidden-node problems, where a station cannot hear another station and collisions result.

cards.q: What do the PHY and MAC layers cover in 802.11?
cards.a: The PHY layer covers OFDM/OFDMA and modulation; the MAC layer covers CSMA/CA and frames; an L2.5 layer handles interop such as WPA.

cards.q: What commands show 802.11 radio, client, and AP status?
cards.a: show ap radio summary, show ap dot11 5ghz summary, show wireless client summary, show ap config general, and show ap monitor.

cards.q: No beacon is seen from an AP, and clients see no network. What is the likely cause and check?
cards.a: The radio is likely disabled. Check the AP radio state with show ap radio summary.

cards.q: The WLAN is slow and association is failing. What are the likely causes?
cards.a: Slow performance is often caused by legacy clients lowering the data rate; association failures are often an authentication mismatch. Check the dot11 rate settings for slow clients and the client authentication for assoc failures.

cards.q: Which 802.11 quick review facts should you remember?
cards.a: Access is CSMA/CA with receiver ACK; frames are management/control/data; n = MIMO, ac = 5 GHz, ax = OFDMA/6 GHz; RTS/CTS solves hidden node; beacons every ~100 ms.
